Republican nominee for New York governor Bruce Blakeman savaged Gov. Kathy Hochul in an exclusive, 20-minute interview with The Post’s Rich Calder this week, branding her a Mamdani “tool.” The 71-year-old Nassau County Executive vowed to reverse the damage the left has done, using political muscle to force the state Legislature and City Hall to kill congestion pricing, flood the streets with cops, and slash income taxes. Q: During Tuesday’s debate, Gov. Hochul brought up President Trump’s name roughly 20 times . . . trying to tie his unpopularity in Democratic New York State – especially NYC – to you. What are you doing to ensure this “Trump the Boogeyman” strategy fails?

Q: You’ve repeatedly said you plan to cut New York’s utility bills in half, if governor. I know you’ve accused Hochul of driving up bills through a “green energy scam” and vowed to let New York produce more gas through fracking, but do you have a clear plan for cutting bills that drastically?

Q: Is Hochul a closet communist or socialist? Why or why not?

Q: A Pollfinity survey released Tuesday says your campaign has narrowed the gap behind Hochul to just 3 points, meaning you’ve gained serious ground in the past few months. Any thoughts as to why?

Q: Are you surprised President Trump continues to embrace the idea of working with Mayor Mamdani?

A: I think government officials have to work with each other, whether they like them or not, and whether they like their policies or not. So, I have to deal with Democratic government officials all the time, so I have no problem with that.

Q: But she never actually did this publicly, so I’m saying do you think she did it behind the scenes? She did not do that publicly.

A: I believe she publicly called for his resignation.

A: Well, I’ve made a public offer to the ownership and the leadership of the New York Jets that we have a site [near the Nassau] Coliseum that we think would be perfect for a football stadium. And basically, to date, the Jets have indicated that they’re perfectly comfortable where they are.

And I will match my record against Kathy Hochul’s any day of the week, because my goal as governor is to make people happy, and she’s done nothing but make New Yorkers miserable.

A car burns at Place de La Republique during a protest against rising living costs in Paris on Saturday. (AP: Emma Da Silva)

Protesters have clashed with police across France during continued nationwide rallies over education and the cost of living.

A government building stormed in Marseille had the anarchy symbol spray painted on walls, while buildings were set alight in Lyon.

The clashes come in the lead up to France's presidential election in April next year.

Protesters clashed with police across France during nationwide rallies over education and the cost of living, as the country heads towards a presidential election.

In Paris, police fired a water cannon and tear gas after hundreds of protesters — most wearing face masks and some setting off fireworks — confronted them at several locations on Saturday.

The tourist office in Lyon was set on fire on Saturday, and offices of French broadcasters CNews and Europe 1 in Paris had windows broken when protesters threw projectiles, French media reported.

"We're taking the Bastille," one demonstrator shouted in Marseille as masked protesters rammed the door of the mayor's offices with security barriers.

The cry is a reference to the 1789 storming of a fortress during the French Revolution.

Protesters scuffle with police during a demonstration against rising living costs in Paris on Saturday. (AP: Emma Da Silva)

Several then entered the town hall, one spray painting an anarchist "A" symbol on an inside wall, before police intervened.

"We're here to protest the deplorable resources allocated to education and against police brutality," said Aude, a masked student who did not give her surname.

Thousands of demonstrators converged for a march through Paris, cutting main roads and prompting authorities to close metro stations in the centre.

The protests are piling pressure on President Emmanuel Macron's government after weeks of student demonstrations turned violent.

The country's Yellow Vest movement, which staged street protests against Mr Macron's government eight years ago over planned fuel tax hikes, had called for the "yellow and youth" demonstrations.

More than 600 demonstrations were planned across France, according to a website set up by organisers.

More than 32,000 protesters took part in some 140 actions nationwide outside Paris shortly after midday on Saturday and police detained more than 160 people nationwide, a source at the interior ministry told AFP.

A masked protester holds a French flag in front of French CRS riot police amid clashes at Place de la Nation.  (Reuters: Yves Herman)

In Paris, where authorities have banned protests around government buildings, the Champs-Elysees shopping avenue and train stations, police detained around 60 people on Saturday morning.

There has been public criticism over the police's perceived disproportionate response.

In the western city of Rennes, around 20 people set up a barricade using trash bins and large pallets on the outskirts of a shopping mall.

Christophe, a 47-year-old carpenter and former Yellow Vest protester who did not give his surname, said he was indignant after seeing what he viewed as police brutality against teenagers in recent weeks.

"We've reached the point where the repression is targeting our own children," he told AFP.

A protester holds a French flag during a demonstration against rising living costs in Lyon on Saturday. (AP: Laurent Cipriani)

"At the end of the month, I have nothing left. Prices are going up but wages aren't," said Franck, a civil servant in his forties who would not give his surname.

Franck was protesting in the central town of Gueret with around 300 people, a quarter of them high school students.

"We can't take it anymore, we're suffocating," he added.

Around 45 per cent of French people are worried about the cost of living and inflation, according to a survey of 2,000 people published earlier this month.

Purchasing power in France has dwindled since 2024, while the price of fuel has soared since the start of the US-Iran war earlier this year.

The eurozone's second largest economy is struggling to reign in its public debt, projected next year to reach more than 120 per cent of GDP, which is double the EU limit of 60 per cent.

Economists say significant debt reduction will come only with major reforms, such as sharply curtailing France's generous pension system.

President Macron on Friday evening called "for calm and respect", adding the right to protest went hand in hand with "respect for people and property".

Jean-Luc Melenchon (right) leader of French far-left opposition party marched in a demonstration by French high school and university students. (Reuters: Sarah Meyssonnier)

France's far-left and far-right parties have both capitalised upon the unrest.

Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the far-left France Unbowed party, has backed the student protests and marched in one demonstration.

Marine Le Pen, who leads in opinion polls for the presidential race, has positioned her National Rally party on the side of the police.

Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer with Anthropic.

“I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.”

Replit sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. Under its partnership with Anthropic, Replit used the AI lab’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly.

Masad’s comments were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.

There is evidence on the company’s website, blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was using Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities.

TechCrunch reached back out to Replit for clarification and will update this story if we hear back.

Masad shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue.

“We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.”

Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures.

“In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.”

This article was updated to article to include more context on Replit using Anthropic’s models.

A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit recently delivered a very disturbing ruling based on decades of legal precedent that have upended efforts to protect children from Child Sexual Abuse Material. The appeals court reluctantly upheld the dismissal of a criminal indictment for possession of AI-generated child pornography — though charges for producing and distributing the disturbing images were not dismissed.

The decision in U.S. v. Anderegg demonstrates the thorny problems caused by the law having to catch up with the rapid pace of new technology: in this case, AI-generated CSAM. But a quarter-century-old concurrence by Justice Clarence Thomas provides a possible constitutional path forward that could prevent the possession of this vile material.

Why was the possession charge dismissed but not the other two? The 7th Circuit said it was bound by several prior Supreme Court decisions, including Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition (2002), which held the mere possession of virtual CSAM was protected by the First Amendment. The earlier case of Stanley v. Georgia (1969) held that individuals have a general right under the First Amendment to possess “obscenity” in the privacy of their home. However, another case, Osborne v. Ohio (1990), said that right did not extend to CSAM depicting actual children.

Here, the defendant created “hyper-realistic images of prepubescent children engaging in sexually explicit acts” with generative AI and distributed them to a 15-year-old boy through Instagram. Both of those acts remain criminal; the only question the court considered was whether the possession alone was criminal.

In Free Speech Coalition, the case most relevant to the issue of possession of AI-generated CSAM, the Supreme Court looked at a new federal statute, the Child Pornography Prevention Act of 1996, which extended the ban on CSAM involving images of actual children to “computer-generated” images. The court ruled that the First Amendment prevented the government from banning possession of CSAM that was not based on images or pictures of actual children.

Many people, including the 7th Circuit judges who ruled in this defendant’s favor, are rightfully concerned that the case law could mean the normalization of AI-generated CSAM. The difference between 2002 — when Free Speech Coalition was decided — and today is the exponential development of the realism of computer-generated images.

The government argued to the 7th Circuit that the rapid advance in technology in the 23 years since Ashcroft has made it “increasingly difficult to distinguish between virtual CSAM and CSAM produced with actual children.” In 2002, said the government, the “internet was ‘still more of a prototype than a finished product.’”

The appellate judges in Anderegg considered that argument, saying that “[g]iven the ever-accelerating march of imaging-generation technology, we have some misgivings about applying Free Speech Coalition here,” but the judges were “dutybound to follow” that precedent.

Significantly, two judges, both Biden appointees, urged the Supreme Court to revisit the issue. In a concurrence that was joined by Judge Joshua Kolar, Judge John Lee (who also wrote the opinion for the unanimous three-judge panel) wrote that “given the significant advances in computer-generated image technology, particularly in the field of artificial intelligence, we would benefit from additional guidance from the Supreme Court regarding the intersection between the First Amendment and virtual CSAM.”

Lee and Kolar also noted that several Supreme Court justices in the Free Speech Coalition predicted the problem of the rapid advance of technology. In a partial dissent, former Justice Sandra Day O’Connor wrote that “rapidly advancing technology soon will make it all but impossible to” enforce prohibitions of actual CSAM and computer-generated images that “bear a remarkable likeness to actual human beings.” In an opinion concurring in the judgment, Justice Clarence Thomas agreed, warning that “[i]f technological advances thwart prosecution of ‘unlawful speech,’ the Government may well have a compelling interest in barring or otherwise regulating some narrow category of ‘lawful speech’ in order to enforce effectively laws against pornography made through the abuse of real children.”

As Lee and Kolar conclude, “that day may have arrived.”

If that day has arrived, then we are faced with the dilemma of balancing First Amendment rights with the justified interest in preventing child exploitation. As AI-generated CSAM becomes harder to distinguish from CSAM of a real child, the task before the courts becomes a technical question of whether an image can be proven to be AI or not. This technical question is a constantly moving goal post that muddles constitutional legal principles and raises difficult questions.

What should the courts do, and does the Supreme Court need to revisit this problem? Should the law expand its reach further into the home and criminalize all CSAM possession, regardless of whether it is or isn’t AI-generated?

Preserving the legal distinction between real life and virtual reality is important. The basis for the state having the power to criminalize CSAM possession within the home is to combat the harm imposed by its creation on real children. The Supreme Court in Free Speech Coalition rejected arguments that virtual CSAM necessarily grows the market for real CSAM, questioning why an individual would “risk prosecution by abusing real children if fictional, computerized images would suffice.” How the material was made must be considered.

Lee and Kolar raise concerns that if an AI’s training material includes real CSAM, then demand for the AI’s outputs feeds demand for the abuse itself. Even if that premise is true, the real CSAM is already illegal — possessing it, for any purpose, is a crime — and they concede that the factual record in the Anderegg case was not sufficient to make a judgment on this issue. Ultimately, the technical argument is a red herring; child pornography law ought to be grounded in preventing harm to real children, not in policing a model’s training set.

The distinction between real and non-real CSAM was important in the Supreme Court’s analysis. Free Speech Coalition left untouched the ban on images altered from real children, because those implicate real victims.

If we want to maintain the distinction between real and synthetic images and not fully reject Ashcroft, then a possible solution is to prohibit AI-generated CSAM (not based on real children) that is “indistinguishable” from real imagery. In other words, images that a reasonable person is unable to conclude are not those of an actual minor. An obscene image a reasonable viewer cannot tell from a photograph of a real child can mask a real victim; a cartoon cannot.

This is not a standard dependent on whether technology exists to determine whether an image is of a real person. Rather, it is a standard that rests solely on the law’s purpose of protecting real children, and it allows imagery no ordinary viewer would mistake for a photograph or video of a real child to remain lawful within the home.

SENATORS INTRODUCE BIPARTISAN BILL TO PURGE CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE FROM AI TRAINING DATA

This standard would narrowly tailor the imposition on free speech within the home, as Justice Thomas suggested in Free Speech Coalition, while maintaining the state’s role in protecting minors from dangerous abuse.

While the Anderegg ruling is disturbing and Supreme Court precedent has closed off the broadest legal remedy for stopping this noxious digital misbehavior, there is a way to remedy the problem. We can protect children while still preserving First Amendment rights. It only takes the Supreme Court and potentially Congress to recognize it.

Everybody Watches The White House, But These Local Elections Could Have More Power Over Your Life

The White House gets most of the political attention, but some of the decisions that hit closest to home are being made by people whose names you might not even recognize.

Everybody has something to say about what’s happening in Washington. Political debates take over social media, national elections dominate the news, and presidential decisions spark conversations across the country. Meanwhile, the people deciding who gets prosecuted, how county jails operate, what happens inside local courtrooms, and how public schools function often receive a fraction of that attention.

That’s why local elections deserve just as much attention as national politics, especially when the decisions can affect your everyday life more directly.

On November 3, 2026, Americans will head to the polls for the midterm elections. While congressional races will attract much of the spotlight, some voters will also have opportunities to choose local officials who exercise significant authority over their communities.

The district attorney, sheriff, judges, and school board members may not have the national recognition of someone in the White House. However, their decisions can determine what happens when someone is arrested, whether a person remains behind bars while awaiting trial, and what resources children receive in school.

One Georgia community already showed just how much those local positions can matter.

In November 2020, voters in Georgia’s Brunswick Judicial Circuit removed longtime District Attorney Jackie Johnson from office following widespread criticism of how authorities handled the killing of Ahmaud Arbery.

According to Georgia Public Broadcasting, Johnson lost her reelection bid to Keith Higgins, a former prosecutor who ran as an independent. His campaign gained support as public frustration grew over the handling of Arbery’s case.

Arbery, a 25-year-old Black man, was shot and killed on February 23, 2020, after being pursued by Gregory and Travis McMichael in a Georgia neighborhood. Gregory McMichael had previously worked as an investigator in Johnson’s office.

The killing sparked national outrage, particularly after video of the encounter became public and questions intensified about why the men involved had not been arrested.

According to the Georgia Bureau of Investigation, Gregory and Travis McMichael were arrested on May 7, 2020, more than two months after Arbery was killed. State investigators had taken over the case just days earlier.

Johnson had recused herself because of her office’s connection to Gregory McMichael. However, criticism surrounding the initial investigation and the actions of local prosecutors continued to grow.

The backlash eventually reached the ballot box.

Georgia Public Broadcasting reported that people attending protests over Arbery’s killing also helped collect signatures to get Higgins on the ballot. Voters wanted another option for the office responsible for prosecuting crimes in their communities.

In February 2025, the criminal case against Johnson ended in her favor. According to the Associated Press, a judge ordered her acquittal on a misdemeanor obstruction charge because prosecutors had not presented evidence that she directed police against making an arrest. The judge also dismissed a felony oath of office charge because of problems with the indictment.

Johnson denied wrongdoing, while Arbery’s parents maintained their belief that she had played a role in protecting the men responsible for their son’s death.

But the election had already happened.

Voters did not need to wait for a criminal trial to decide whether they wanted different leadership in the district attorney’s office. They exercised their authority through the voting process.

That example illustrates why paying attention to local elections is about much more than recognizing familiar political names.

District attorneys hold enormous power within the criminal justice system. They help decide which cases move forward, what criminal charges prosecutors pursue, whether plea agreements are offered, and what sentences prosecutors request.

Those decisions can influence whether someone faces years in prison or receives an opportunity to resolve a case without going to trial.

Yet many voters know far more about national political figures than the prosecutors responsible for making those decisions in their own counties.

A 2015 analysis from the Women Donors Network examined 2,437 elected prosecutors who held office in 2014 and found that 95% were white. The research also cited a study by Wake Forest University law professor Ronald Wright showing that 85% of incumbent prosecutors ran unopposed.

Those figures are historical and do not describe the current composition of prosecutor offices. Still, they highlight longstanding concerns about representation and how often voters have meaningful choices in these powerful elections.

And prosecutors are only part of the picture.

Consider the county sheriff.

When people think about law enforcement, they often focus on police departments. However, sheriffs in many counties oversee jails, supervise deputies, and establish policies that affect people who are arrested or detained.

For example, Miami County’s government in Indiana identifies the sheriff as an elected constitutional officer responsible for several duties, including caring for the county jail and the people held inside it.

That means decisions involving jail operations, detention conditions, staffing, and enforcement priorities can fall under the authority of someone chosen through local elections.

For families with loved ones in custody, those responsibilities are anything but distant political issues. They can influence everyday experiences during some of the most difficult moments in a person’s life.

Then there are the judges.

While prosecutors decide which cases to pursue, judges make decisions involving bail, courtroom procedures, criminal sentences, and legal disputes. Depending on the jurisdiction and type of case, a judge’s ruling can affect whether someone returns home while awaiting trial or remains in custody.

Many state judges are selected through elections, while others face retention votes that allow voters to decide whether they should continue serving.

According to Utah’s official voter information website, the state uses judicial retention elections in which voters choose yes or no on whether an appointed judge should remain in office.

Utah’s 2026 judicial ballots include retention contests for positions across its court system, according to state election filings. These decisions receive nowhere near the attention of the White House, despite their direct connection to the administration of justice.

The same issue applies to school board elections, especially for parents.

Families spend years debating education policies at the national level, but school boards frequently have direct authority over district budgets, educational programs, school policies, and the resources available to students.

In Florida, for example, state law gives district school boards responsibility for operating, controlling, and supervising public schools within their districts, subject to state law.

That authority can affect everything from educational opportunities and discipline policies to funding decisions for music, athletics, and other school programs.

A school board member may never become a trending topic online. Still, their decisions can influence the classroom your child walks into every morning.

None of this means the White House is unimportant. Federal leadership shapes national laws, economic policy, government funding, and decisions with consequences throughout the country.

But national authority does not eliminate the influence of local government.

In fact, the two often operate together. Federal and state policies establish broad rules, while local officials make important decisions about enforcement, implementation, and the services residents actually experience.

That distinction becomes particularly important during the 2026 midterm elections.

Not every district attorney, sheriff, judge, or school board position will appear on the November 3 ballot. Election schedules and the offices being contested vary by state, county, and school district. Some local races take place in other election years.

That’s why voters should know exactly which positions are being decided where they live rather than assuming every community has the same ballot.

According to USAGov’s official voter guidance, sample ballots allow voters to review the candidates and ballot measures they will encounter before heading to the polls. Voter guides can also provide information about candidates’ experience and positions.

That preparation can make a significant difference when someone reaches an unfamiliar name or a judicial retention question.

Look beyond campaign advertisements and party labels. Research how candidates have handled their responsibilities, what policies they support, and what authority their offices actually hold.

For prosecutors, that might mean examining their approach to criminal charges and accountability. For sheriffs, it could involve jail management and public safety practices. For judges, voters can review professional evaluations where available. For school board candidates, their positions on education funding and district priorities may be especially relevant.

The larger point is that political power does not begin and end in Washington.

The White House may dominate the conversation, but local government is often where families encounter the consequences of public policy firsthand.

And when voters overlook those elections, they risk paying less attention to some of the officials making the most immediate decisions about their communities.

The people controlling your local courts, county jails, and public schools may never become household names, but your vote helps determine who holds that power and how it is used.

Poli Girl, known by her pen name poligirlsayswhat, is a political journalist and contributor for Baller Alert covering the intersection of politics, culture, and social impact. Her work focuses on breaking down complex policy, elections, and major headlines into clear, accessible insights that connect national decisions to everyday life.

With a focus on accountability, media literacy, and the real-world impact of political power, she brings a culturally aware perspective to stories that shape public discourse, particularly within underrepresented communities. Her reporting and commentary center on transparency, truth, and the influence of government decisions on daily life.

Following increased public attention and threats tied to her coverage of the administration, she has chosen to maintain a lower public profile while continuing her work. Despite this, her voice remains a consistent and trusted source of insight for readers seeking clarity in an increasingly complex political landscape.

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Flu season usually builds in late fall, but this year it’s getting a jump start. During the week ending September 26, 3.4 percent of respiratory samples tested by clinical labs came back positive for flu, according to CDC data. That’s roughly seven times the rate at the same point last year, when 0.5 percent tested positive.

The early uptick is concentrated in Western states. In Washington, the share of emergency department visits diagnosed as flu climbed from 0.25 percent in late August to 1.34 percent in the week ending October 3, a more than fivefold increase in six weeks. California and Arizona are seeing elevated activity too. “This particular year, it appears to be starting early — like right now,” said Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of preventive medicine and infectious diseases at Vanderbilt Health, who says patients at clinics in his area are already testing positive.

Flu starting in the West isn’t unusual or predictive. “There’s nothing unusual about flu starting in the West Coast and moving east,” Schaffner said. It can start almost anywhere; recent seasons have come out of the Southeast or Midwest first. An early start also doesn’t mean a bad season. The CDC’s 2026-2027 outlook projects moderate severity, though with only low-to-moderate confidence.

Seasonal flu comes in three subtypes: two influenza A strains (H1N1 and H3N2) and one influenza B lineage called Victoria. Of the influenza A samples subtyped during the week ending September 26, 96 percent were H1N1. Last season a fast-spreading H3N2 variant dominated, and the CDC classified 2025-2026 as highly severe for children, with at least 195 child deaths from flu-related causes.

Schaffner describes influenza A and B as siblings: “They’re very related, but they each have their own individual characteristics.” Influenza A tends to drive the biggest outbreaks early; influenza B strains “kind of smolder along” toward the end. The 96 percent figure is where things stand now, not a forecast for the full season.

Flu is, as Dr. Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, puts it, “a moving target.” The virus mutates constantly, especially in hemagglutinin, the surface protein it uses to latch onto human cells and the main target of flu vaccines. When circulating strains diverge significantly from those in the vaccine formulation, “that usually predicts a more difficult season,” Offit says. Whether this year’s shot is a close match won’t be clear for weeks.

The CDC recommends annual flu vaccination for everyone six months and older. Flu hits hardest in children under five, adults 65 and older, people with chronic health conditions, and pregnant people; tens of thousands of Americans die of flu each season, and serious infections can cause pneumonia, sepsis, and heart or brain complications.

The shot works better when you get it at the right time. The CDC advises against vaccinating in July or August for most adults because protection can wane over a long season. With flu arriving ahead of schedule, “October is the ideal time to get vaccinated, and even more so right now,” Schaffner said. Full protection takes about two weeks to build after the shot.

Effectiveness varies. In terms of flu cases that send people to the doctor, vaccines have been 29 to 56 percent effective over the past decade, per CDC estimates. They do better against severe illness. Schaffner puts the calculus directly: they work best at “keeping you out of the hospital, keeping you out of the intensive care unit, and keeping you out of the cemetery.”

Adults 50 and older have a new option this year. The FDA approved mFlusiva in August, the first mRNA flu vaccine. Traditional shots contain purified viral proteins. The mRNA version delivers genetic instructions that the body’s cells use to produce those same proteins themselves, then break down. “It cannot influence human genetic material,” Schaffner said. The result, according to Offit: “you’re less likely to get symptomatic disease.”

For adults 65 and older, the CDC still prefers high-dose or adjuvanted shots. Adjuvanted vaccines include an extra ingredient that prompts a stronger immune response.

Topic:Gymnastics

Jamie Glen Cannon did not receive a conviction after pleading guilty to assaulting two female teenage athletes at a Sunshine Coast club. (ABC News: Owen Jacques)

A long-time gymnastics coach has received a fine and no conviction after pleading guilty to assaulting two female teenage athletes.

Jamie Glen Cannon faced four charges of common assault. The court heard there was no sexual intent in the offending.

Cannon was given a single fine of $2,500 and ordered to pay each teenager $1,000 in compensation. No conviction was recorded.

A gymnastics coach with more than 30 years' experience has avoided conviction and instead been ordered to pay a fine after assaulting two teenage female athletes.

Over the length of his career, Jamie Glen Cannon, 49, has trained athletes at clubs on the Sunshine Coast, in Cairns, and at Brisbane Grammar School.

Mr Cannon was sentenced in Maroochydore District Court last week, after pleading guilty to four charges of common assault against the two teen gymnasts, each aged between 13 and 16.

Jamie Cannon has coached athletes at clubs on the Sunshine Coast, Cairns and at Brisbane Grammar School over his 30-year career. (ABC News: Alex Papp)

Crown prosecutor Alex Stark described Cannon's behaviour as "a breach of trust, both professional and personal" and tendered an agreed statement of facts about the offending.

The court heard Cannon was a senior coach at a Sunshine Coast club when the incidents occurred in 2022 and 2023.

The two girls were under his supervision as athletes.

One of the assault charges related to Cannon smacking the bottom of a 13-year-old as she performed handstands with other gymnasts at the club.

One athlete's victim impact statement said the offending led to her "quitting gymnastics entirely". (Pexels: Ivan Samkov / CC licence)

Three more offences occurred at the same club, involving Cannon touching and rubbing the inner thigh of a second athlete, aged 15 at the time.

The court heard that in one interaction, Cannon asked the teenager if she wore make-up, told her she was pretty, then put his hand on her inner thigh.

In another, he asked if he could touch the teenager's leggings, and before she could respond, he put his hand on her knee.

The fourth charge involved Cannon approaching the 15-year-old as she prepared to coach a class, standing in between her legs before placing his hands on her knees and rubbing her thighs as she attempted to move away.

The court heard it was accepted that Cannon's behaviour had "no sexual intent".

The 15-year-old athlete's victim impact statement was read to the court at his sentencing by Mr Stark.

The teenager wrote that the offending led to her "quitting gymnastics entirely".

She described problems falling asleep and how it damaged "many friendships", particularly at the gymnastics club.

"[It] affected the development of a romantic relationship with partners due to fear and sensitivity to certain actions and situations," Mr Stark read to the court.

If you have more information about this story, please contact Owen Jacques at jacques.owen@abc.net.au.

Mr Stark said there was a "vulnerability" in the situation because the teenagers were under his supervision.

He said both teenagers had been clear about their boundaries to Cannon, including the request not to be touched.

Cannon declined to be interviewed by police.

The court heard he has not been involved with the sport since being charged.

Cannon's lawyer Ambyr Cousen described how her client had been involved with the sport for 30 years both as an employee and as a volunteer, including as a committee member with Gymnastics Queensland (GQ).

"He has won a number of awards for peer service within that industry," Ms Cousen told the court.

Cannon was working with Brisbane Grammar School as a senior coach in 2019 when he received GQ's Individual Service Award for his service to gymnastics in Queensland.

He also spent more than a decade leading GQ's Men's Artistic Gymnastics Sport Committee.

Ms Cousen also supplied the court with several character references for her client.

Cannon provided a written apology to the court for his actions, and offered to pay $1,000 to each of the victims as compensation.

Jamie Cannon was sentenced on four counts of common assault in the Maroochydore District Court last week. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Owen Jacques)

In sentencing, Judge Amanda McDonnell told Cannon he treated "these young, vulnerable girls in a way that they didn't wish to be touched".

"I have no doubt that they looked up to you for guidance," Judge McDonnell said.

Cannon was ordered to pay a single fine of $2,500 for the four offences, plus the promised compensation.

No conviction was recorded.

A once frail Labrador retriever puppy at a Mississippi animal shelter has become a hero search-and-rescue dog in disaster zones after being adopted by his handler.

Christy Bormann, a search-and-rescue dog handler in Texas, saw pictures of the puppy online after he was taken in as a stray and immediately felt kinship with the canine, The Washington Post reported.

“I just knew that he was going to be the next partner for me,” said Bormann, who named the dog Canyon because he loves to dig holes.

Bormann noticed Canyon had a love affair with playing fetch and would grab anything he could and drop it in front of her and the shelter employees. Over two years, Bormann worked with the dog, helping him gain weight and honing his love of fetch into skills needed for becoming a working dog.

Bormann was sure Canyon’s energy and strong sense of smell would help her work natural disaster sites and locate missing people.

Within the past several years, Canyon has helped with dozens of search-and-rescue missions, including the Texas floods in 2025, which killed more than 100 people, including children at Camp Mystic, according to the report. The pup also assisted with rescue operations during Hurricane Helene in 2024 and the 2023 Maui wildfires.

“He could run through an entire room full of his favorite peanut butter cups, would not even look at them, and is only looking for that target scent,” 48-year-old Bormann told the publication.

Bormann carries a squeaky bunny toy for the 7-year-old working dog for him to play fetch with as a reward after a mission.

The work is devastating but critical to helping authorities give answers to grieving families: Canyon specifically helps locate people who have died in natural disasters.

On Thursday, the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA) honored Canyon as the dog of the year, in part for his work on the Texas floods.

Bormann said she has her dogs retired around the age of 9, when their energy begins to flag. She said she keeps her dogs disciplined while they are active working dogs, making sure they follow her commands and sleep away from her room — but they get more privileges after retirement.

“When he’s retired, he will get to sleep in bed full-time,” Bormann said.

Susan Collins, Troy Jackson clashed on Tuesday evening over views on whether ICE needs reform or abolishment after the death of Sebastián Durán Guerrero.

Fierce disagreement broke out on the debate stage on Tuesday evening as Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, defended her record against accusations that she had enabled the death of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero at the hands of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Troy Jackson, her Democratic opponent, argued Collins had facilitated the deadly encounter on the three-month anniversary of the incident by funding what he described as a "rogue agency."

"Look, Senator Collins paid for the bullets and at Donald Trump's command. Now she wants credit for not pulling the trigger," Jackson said, referring to the roughly $66 billion in funding for immigration enforcement agencies included in the Secure America Act, a party-line bill that extended provisions for the agency through the end of Trump’s term.

TRUMP TAKES ICE SHUTDOWNS OFF THE TABLE WITH SIGNATURE ON KEY $70B BILL

Former state Senator Troy Jackson, a Democrat from Maine and gubernatorial candidate, speaks during a Fighting Oligarchy event with Graham Platner. (Sophie Park/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"That's the choice on this stage. A senator who helps Donald Trump hurt Maine then tells us how concerned she is, or somebody who will stand up against him before another family in Maine has to pay the price."

Notably, not all of the funding described by Jackson was set aside for ICE. The package set aside $26 billion for border security operations under Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and $38.5 for ICE. The package also included $5 billion for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) general funds.

Guerrero’s shooting has become a flash point in Trump’s immigration enforcement push, especially in the Maine Senate race where Democrats have used his death to illustrate broader critiques of Collins: that her occasional willingness to break with the majority of the GOP hasn’t meaningfully curbed the administration’s policies. But at the debate on Tuesday evening, the third between Collins and Jackson, Collins pushed back on the narrative, arguing that her power as a Republican senator has been key to implementing a handful of safeguards on an agency that she described as critical to American safety.

"After the Biddeford shooting, I called the Secretary of Homeland Security, [and] met with the acting director and suggested that they prioritize Maine for receipt of these body-worn cameras. And they did. And every ICE agent in the state of Maine and across the country now has the body-worn cameras," Collins said at the debate on Tuesday.

"I increased by 17% the budget for the independent Office of Inspector General," Collins added.

Guerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian national, was fatally shot in Biddeford on July 13 when he tried to flee ICE officers in a vehicle during an operation targeting an illegal immigrant with a final order of removal, according to the Department of Homeland Security.

Guerrero was not the target of the operation.

'SQUAD' MEMBER CALLS DHS 'GREATEST THREAT TO OUR SAFETY' AFTER ICE-INVOLVED SHOOTING

Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate in Maine, is pictured alongside Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images; Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

"The vehicle attempted to flee the scene and, fearing for public safety, an officer discharged his weapon. The driver of the vehicle was struck and emergency services were immediately contacted. He passed away from his injuries," DHS said in a statement at the time.

In Jackson’s estimation, the moment is emblematic of what he described as an agency out of control.

"That is why I believe that this agency is just a rogue agency that's doing Donald Trump's bidding," Jackson said.

"I do believe it's important to get rid of it and take that money and prioritize it into existing law enforcement that actually people believe in."

Like many progressives, Jackson has argued that the agency is beyond the scope of reform, sharing the view of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). The group, which backed Jackson in his gubernatorial bid earlier this year before he became a candidate for Senate, calls the agency "a violent and illegitimate agency."

Jackson has shared almost that exact framing, similarly stating that ICE "is not legitimate law enforcement," in a debate from last Thursday.

Collins disagrees.

On Tuesday, she argued that the agency, although flawed, serves an important role in American law enforcement, pointing out that its role overlaps with many other forms of law enforcement.

"It investigates child trafficking, human trafficking and general child exploitation: drug smuggling, international cartels, financial scams. It recently helped shut down a child pornography ring in the state of Maine. I don't think any of us wants to go back to the days of completely open, uncontrolled borders. saudi-solar-park-proves-brilliant-breedi:
In clearing two hurdles with one bound, Saudi conservationists have turned a large solar farm into a breeding shelter for a vulnerable species of native gazelle.

Located near the Red Sea coastline in a massive, 24,500-square-mile nature reserve, the solar plant is now hosting Arabian sand gazelles, a species of special consideration for wildlife managers.

Though commonly found across the world’s zoos, it’s believed only 3,000 of these small ungulates survive in the wilds of the Arabian Peninsula and Turkiye. Zoos are one thing, but a 250-megawatt solar power installation is another.

The plant serves the Kingdom’s 100% renewably-powered tourist resort, Amaala, but it’s now become the home for 38 gazelles. Spanning 1,200 acres, the wildlife-proof fencing surrounding the arsenal of panels ensures the gazelles can feed, breed, and explore without predation pressure.

The hope is that these several dozen can grow to over 500 which will then be used to reestablish a strong population within the massive reserve.

“Our rewilding goal is to build self-sustaining wildlife populations that can survive in the wild without ongoing human intervention,” said Andrew Zaloumis, the reserve’s director.

“This collaborative innovation not only accelerates that work but also introduces a novel ‘double-green’ framework with global scalability. We are calling it ‘ReWildingVoltaics.’”

Doesn’t really roll off the tongue, but branding is hardly the point.

Along with the sand gazelles, mountain gazelles and Arabian hares were also released into the solar park last October. In May, once it was clear the animals were settling in, male members were added in the hopes of establishing a self-perpetuating population.

It’s not the first idea of doing 2 different things with solar plants. The panels offer easy shade that’s between 8 and 18 degrees cooler than under the Arabian sunshine.

The Saudi Gazette reported that the initiative supports the Saudi Green Initiative targets to protect 30% of the Kingdom’s land and sea and generate 50% of its electricity from renewable sources by 2030.

By AMANDA GOFF

Published:  00:31 AEDT, 14 October 2026   |  Updated:  07:13 AEDT, 14 October 2026

They say living well is the best revenge.

Do you know what I think comes a close second? Having a column and a score to settle. Especially when it involves a well-known TV personality who, to put it bluntly, was absolutely awful to me and continues to enjoy an unblemished reputation.

I know what you're thinking: 'Here's Amanda with another carve-up of a celeb. How can she, of all people, point the finger and accuse someone else of being mean?'

Yes, I write my opinions of people, and they're not always flattering. I know for a fact that I've upset a few people along the way, and I dare say I'll upset a few more. That's an occupational hazard of being paid to have opinions.

But strong opinions are not a licence to twist the knife, and there's a vast difference between skewering the tomfoolery of elites and making another person feel small.

Which brings me to my experience with Sally Bowrey, the squeaky clean Weekend Sunrise news anchor whose treatment of me I haven't forgotten all these years later.

Even after all these years, I haven't forgotten how squeaky clean Weekend Sunrise news anchor Sally Bowrey made me feel on live television. I remember leaving the studio in tears

'I remember the hot studio lights, stumbling over my words as I tried to answer what felt like sneering, aggressive questions that came at me faster than I could gather my thoughts,' writes Amanda Goff

You're maybe wondering why I've decided to bring it up.

Well, as I write this, The Australian's Steve Jackson reports that axed Today show presenter Sarah Abo - who has a reputation for being genuinely lovely - is being wooed by Seven's Melbourne news bulletin. Reading it, I felt compelled to put pen to paper before she joins a network where my own experience was far less pleasant than the public image suggests.

Honestly, it has taken me almost a decade to write this. I've settled scores before, including with Abbie Chatfield, and there are others whose turn may yet come. (Sam Armytage is among them. Unfortunately, my editors and the Mail's lawyers would have collective heart failure if I put those thoughts in print.)

But back to Bowrey. Before my run-in with her, I encountered another Sally - Sally Obermeder - who you might remember as one of the hosts of The Daily Edition. Bowrey occasionally filled in for her.

Before I became Samantha X, I occasionally worked as a freelance producer on Seven's flagship current affairs program, Today Tonight. Obermeder was due to go on maternity leave and I was brought in as a possible replacement. It was a huge job, completely new to me, and I was beyond excited. A dream come true.

But soon after arriving, I got the distinct impression Obermeder didn't like me. That impression resurfaced while writing this column when I discovered she had blocked me on Instagram, possibly years ago.

During my brief time at Today Tonight, I felt increasingly unwelcome and my confidence gradually evaporated. I ended up in tears speaking to a female boss about how I felt. Eventually, the job I'd been so excited about came to nothing. No one likes a squeaky wheel.

Don't get me wrong. There were some lovely women at Seven: Chris Bath, Nat Barr, the chief of staff, and a handful of other producers who were always real, authentic and refreshing.

Before my run-in with Bowrey, I had a bad experience at Today Tonight after being drafted in as a possible maternity replacement for Sally Obermeder (pictured). Soon after arriving, I got the distinct feeling Obermeder didn't like me. The influencer now has me blocked on Instagram

And I'm no snowflake. I've worked in some of the toughest newsrooms in London, dealt with screaming editors, ruthless journalists and more than my fair share of difficult personalities. Piers Morgan was one of my first bosses.

But at Seven, for the first time in my professional life, I found myself second-guessing my own worth. To this day, I've wondered what I might have said or done wrong.

Perhaps Obermeder and others remember things differently. I'm sure she has her own reasons for blocking me. I can only tell you how I felt at the time.

Fast forward a year or so and a lot had changed. I farewelled 9-to-5 journalism and became Samantha X. Around the same time, Seven launched a new daytime show, The Daily Edition, with Obermeder as one of its presenters.

And boy, did I have a great story: glossy magazine writer becomes high-class escort. Instead of putting the news together, I became a walking headline.

Seven's Sunday Night ran the exclusive on me and promoted my memoir, Hooked.

I became media fodder. For months, producers from The Daily Edition emailed asking me to come on as a guest. My answer was always the same: no.

And I was honest about why. After my tough time at Today Tonight, I didn't want to be face to face with Obermeder on live television.

Until one day another invitation landed in my inbox. Obermeder was going on holiday. Would I reconsider if someone else interviewed me?

That someone was Sally Bowrey.

I'd never heard of her. I agreed. I had an escort agency and another book to promote, and it seemed a safe bet.

How wrong I was.

Amanda is pictured during her younger years as a journalist, before she became Samantha X

I'd agreed to an interview with one Sally to avoid the potential awkwardness of being interviewed by the other - but what I hadn't anticipated was walking straight into what felt, to me, like an ambush.

Years later, I don't remember much about those five or so minutes on live television with Bowrey, but I do remember how they made me feel: humiliated, embarrassed, upset, tearful and angry at myself for agreeing to it.

I'd done plenty of live interviews, both as Samantha and Amanda. During my time at Seven, I was a beauty expert on The Morning Show, sharing the studio with the lovely Larry Emdur and Kylie Gillies many times. They were, and still are, consummate professionals.

But with Bowrey, it felt like a completely different story. I'd quit my desk job to become an escort. I accepted that not everyone would approve of my life choices. But it felt as though I was being questioned by police on suspicion of murder.

I remember the hot studio lights, stumbling over my words as I tried to answer what felt like sneering, aggressive questions that came at me faster than I could gather my thoughts.

'Couldn't you just ask for flexi hours?' Bowrey said after I explained that one of the reasons I became Samantha was to achieve a better work-life balance. The question seemed to assume that every workplace simply grants such requests on demand.

Before I could recover, the interview was over and I was left untangling my microphone, fighting back tears before fleeing the studio.

Friends who watched called to see if I was OK. 'That was pretty brutal,' one said.

I don't know whether Sarah Abo (right) is bound for Seven or weighing up other career paths after being axed from Today. But my gut tells me she's far too nice for that place

I wasn't expecting a fireside chat. I was a journalist and knew how it worked. Bowrey wasn't there to stroke my ego. But this was daytime TV, not 60 Minutes. I was an author and escort, not El Chapo.

There is a difference between asking tough questions and leaving someone feeling the way I did that day.

While the past is the past, I've never forgotten how I felt being interviewed by Bowrey and my ill-fated stint at Today Tonight.

Since then, Obermeder has traded television for lifestyle influencing. I noted with interest two recent, unflattering stories about her appeared in the Telegraph - a paper that once breathlessly reported her attending the opening of an envelope.

Bowrey is still at Seven. Woman's Day referred to her this week as 'the beloved Weekend Sunrise star'.

I don't know whether Sarah Abo is bound for Seven or weighing up other career paths after being axed from Today while on maternity leave. But my gut tells me she's far too nice for that place.

In the world of daytime television, it's not always the ratings or the bosses you need to watch. Sometimes it's the hosts sitting right beside you.

A Channel Seven spokesperson told the Daily Mail: 'Having reviewed the footage, we stand by the interview and the questions asked.'

The agency’s ambitious moon base plans have a big question mark

Ned Potter is an IEEE Spectrum contributing editor.

Firefly Aerospace’s Blue Ghost 2 mission aims in 2027 to be the first U.S. spacecraft to land on the far side of the moon.

At Firefly Aerospace in Texas, engineers have been doing what NASA’s chief, Jared Isaacman, likes to call “the near-impossible.” The Firefly team has been assembling Blue Ghost Mission 2, a robotic spacecraft intended to land on the far side of the moon in 2027.

No U.S. spacecraft has ever gone there. Not very many have landed on the near side, either, for that matter. Blue Ghost 2 has thousands of potential failure points and there is almost no room for error. Two ships sent by a competitor, Houston-based Intuitive Machines, reached the moon’s near side in 2024 and 2025 but fell over on landing and returned little useful data. Another mission,  Peregrine Mission One by Pittsburgh-based Astrobotic Technology in 2024, missed the moon entirely because a single helium valve wouldn’t seat properly.

In summary: Moon landings are supremely hard. So far, since Project Apollo ended in 1972, United States spacecraft have landed intact exactly…once.

And now NASA, answering a White House executive order to start building a moon base by decade’s end, says it plans something like 70 lunar landings over 10 years— with 45 of them by 2032. Which raises a major question: How will the U.S. pick up the pace so dramatically?

Carefully, that’s how—carefully, but with all deliberate speed. NASA and its political supporters in Washington frequently cite competition from the Chinese space program, which says it plans its own base near the lunar south pole in the 2030s.

Carlos García-Galán is NASA’s moon base program manager, and his team has laid out a plan with three phases. Phase one, between now and 2029, may involve the near-impossible—putting spacecraft on the moon—but landings need to become regular and low-risk. While the one successful landing so far happens to have been by Firefly (Blue Ghost Mission 1, in March 2025) it’s better to have multiple options. NASA says it expects at least half a dozen companies to try to make landings by the end of 2029. It’s called for seven landings in 2027 and another seven in 2028, just for starters.

“We’re not reaching for the home run on the first swing,” says García-Galán. “We have very specific goals, and the first objectives are achieving high-reliability access to the surface.”

If that succeeds, phase two, between 2029 and 2032, would include the first infrastructure—power systems, communications networks, perhaps the first pressurized rover for astronauts, supplied by Japan’s space agency.

Finally, in phase three, astronauts from NASA’s Artemis project would start to spend extended periods at the base. There would probably be fewer but bigger supply missions over time; NASA initially projected it would have to land 4,000 kilograms of equipment in phase one, 60,000 kg in phase two, and 150,000 kg in phase three, with landing ships large enough by then to carry up to 8,000 kg at a time.

A 3D rendering from NASA shows what a near-term lunar base may look like, something the agency hopes to achieve by the early 2030s.NASA

NASA’s business approach, for more than a decade, has been to let private companies run actual missions where practical; NASA acts as a “customer,” providing basic funding and sending payloads on each flight. Firefly, Intuitive Machines, and Jeff Bezos’s company Blue Origin already have contracts with NASA, with many more to follow. The more options, NASA says, the better.

“Let’s not invest $1 billion in just one thing,” says García-Galán. “Let’s invest $1 billion in 10 things and see which ones work and use that in phase two.”

There is a survival-of-the-fittest quality to the moon base plan. Companies are given contracts of US $100 to $200 million to execute moon missions; for the most part, there will be no government bailouts if they run behind or have technical problems. That means there will undoubtedly be winners and losers: In July, NASA and the nonprofit Draper Laboratory agreed to cancel a contract for a landing attempt; the mission had been targeted for 2025 but was running behind by at least five years.

Five years is obviously not good enough when you’re trying to put down roots near the lunar south pole before China does. NASA is pressing companies to get missions going in two years or even less. In June it signed contracts with three companies—Astrobotic, Firefly, and Intuitive Machines—to try to send landing missions in 2028.

“It’s lit a fire under a lot of people to dream a little bit bigger and go a little bit further,” says Kevin Scholtes, a future systems architect at Firefly. “It’s a lot more exciting, what the future looks like, but it’s a lot more hectic.”

On 22 September, Firefly finished a new cleanroom in Texas, four times as large as its existing space, making it possible to run what it called “a dedicated assembly line” and build up to 12 Blue Ghost landers at once. It’s hardly alone.

“I have personally visited over 15 actual or could-be moon base vendors,” García-Galán says, “and every place I go there’s the main building where they’re doing their current work—and then there’s a building under construction next door because instead of being able to make one they’re going to be able to make four.”

NASA should be, if you’ll pardon the pun, over the moon about all this activity: If companies from Florida to California are competing for its business, they presumably drive down prices and speed up their work. But it cuts both ways. A corporation may set big, idealistic goals, but it also needs to run a profit. At least one company, Masten Space Systems, was hired for an early landing mission, and then, after four years’ effort, went bankrupt.

A much bigger potential headache is Elon Musk’s SpaceX, the unrivaled rocket giant. Its Falcon 9 makes several launches a week, often carrying other companies’ spacecraft for a fee. But SpaceX, which wants to focus on its giant Starship and its efforts in artificial intelligence, has told people in the space community that it wants to retire the Falcon 9 in a few years.

“We definitely want to move from the older technology to the newer technology,” said Gwynne Shotwell, the president of SpaceX under Musk, at a business summit in Los Angeles on 14 September. “If we don’t obsolete our own products and services, someone’s going to find a way to obsolete them for us.”

That leaves everyone else, including NASA, in a bind. Nobody else launches remotely as often. Blue Origin has been building a super-rocket called New Glenn—but one blew up in May, not only destroying the rocket but its one launch pad at Cape Canaveral. Rebuilding is in progress—with NASA rooting for them because Blue Origin and SpaceX are the two competitors to make astronaut landing ships for Artemis missions.

As people at NASA often say, this is a “high risk, high reward” business. But the more businesslike the moon base effort can be, the better. Lunar landing ships, historically, have demanded the most exacting, mission-specific engineering. If a moon base is to succeed (presuming it’s not cancelled outright by a future administration), NASA will need its private-enterprise partners to turn landings into something routine, mass-produced, like a Falcon 9 launch.

Firefly’s Scholtes, for one, says it can happen. He points that while the first airplanes were handcrafted, within a couple of decades one could buy an airplane as a kit.

But it won’t be simple, he says: “It’s the nature of the space industry that the physics is just barely easy enough to be possible.”

Ned Potter is an IEEE Spectrum contributing editor and a New York-based writer who spent more than 25 years as an ABC News and CBS News correspondent covering science, technology, space, and the environment.
family-sells-650-acres-east-texas-lake-s:
A “gem” of a landscape in eastern Texas has been sold by its multigenerational owners for the purpose of becoming a state park.

The property is the longest remaining, contiguous piece of land on Lake Palestine’s shore, and contains pine woods, short bluffs, wetlands, and a pecan orchard that will all soon be open for camping, kayaking, and other forms of recreation.

Sat across 650 acres in Henderson County, the property has for 80 years been owned by the Pollard Family, which built a business growing pecans there up until present day when the current owner, Sam Pollard, decided to put it on the market for public or private conservation purposes.

“This land is part of my soul,” Pollard, who’s also president of Texas Pecan Nursery, said in a statement. “It means a lot to me that we can leave a legacy for people to enjoy.”

The final price was a largely ceremonial pittance of just $1 million—paid by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Foundation nonprofit which buys land that it believes could become Texas State Park land and holds it until the authorities can afford to buy it off them.

“Opportunities to protect a property like this don’t come along very often, and when they do, timing is critical,” said Anne Brown, executive director of the Texas Parks and Wildlife Foundation, the statement. “TPWF was able to step in and secure this land now so it can ultimately become a place where generations of Texans can enjoy the outdoors.”

The property offers significant potential for both conservation and outdoor recreation. Lake Palestine reaches depths of 58 feet and is popular for boating, paddling, swimming and fishing for bass, catfish, and sunfish. Future park visitors will also enjoy scenic blufftop lake views, wildlife and bird watching, and the property’s existing pecan orchard. It also provides habitat for white-tailed deer, bobcats, waterfowl and a variety of woodland and water-dependent birds.

The statement details that the foundation will hold the property until the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department can acquire it in late 2027, when additional funding from the Centennial Parks Conservation Fund becomes available. The fund was authorized several years ago to expand and improve the state park system and recreation opportunities offered therein.

MORE STORIES LIKE THIS: Instead of Taking Millions for Their Land, Texas Family Makes a Park Instead

“We are excited to add this East Texas gem to the Texas State Park system,” said Rodney Franklin, director of Texas State Parks at TPWD. “Families will be able to enjoy lake recreation on Lake Palestine, along with the pecan trees that are a signature of the property. We are grateful to our partners, the Texas Parks and Wildlife Foundation, and to owner Sam Pollard and his family who have generously allowed this special slice of the Pineywoods to be accessible for generations of Texans.”

TEXAS REC: Pioneer is First to Cross Texas Along His New xTx Trail – 1,500 Miles Devised for Hikers, Cyclists and Horses

The department plans to open the future park in phases, beginning with guided access, followed by day use and eventually full day and overnight access. After it purchases the property from the foundation, the department will invite public input to discuss options for the future park.

Once developed, planned amenities include hike and bike trails, traditional and primitive campsites, day-use areas and lakefront access. Habitat restoration will also be an important part of preparing the property for its future as a state park.

The 87-year-old pensioner in Spain whose eviction from her lifelong home sparked nationwide protests has died. María del Carmen Abascal, better known as Maricarmen, died on Wednesday just hours before she was set to sign a new rental agreement. She was forcibly removed from her Madrid apartment last month on a stretcher after the private investment company that owns the building hiked her rent. After massive public outcry, the landlord had agreed to allow her back into her apartment.

Independent Spanish journalist María Carrión says that although Maricarmen’s story galvanized much of the country, evictions like hers are “a daily occurrence” in Spain.

“Rents have gone up 80% in the last 10 years, while salaries have not kept up,” Carrión says. “Young people cannot leave their homes. They cannot become independent or start families. And this is what people are trying to change from the street.”

NERMEEN SHAIKH: We begin today’s show in Spain. Maricarmen has died. She’s the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her home of 70 years in Madrid sparked mass protests across Spain. In September, she was forcibly removed from her apartment on a stretcher after the private investment company which owns the building hiked her rent. After massive public outcry, the landlord had agreed to allow her back into her apartment. María Carmen Abascal died on Wednesday just hours before she was set to sign a new rental agreement.

On Wednesday, protesters in Madrid gathered to shout “murderers” outside the Madrid parliament.

PROTESTERS: ¡Asesinos! ¡Asesinos! ¡Asesinos! ¡Asesinos!

AMY GOODMAN: Protesters in Madrid, Spain, responded with sadness and anger over the death of 87-year-old Maricarmen.

DIANA: [translated] She’s a woman who died of heartbreak. They killed her through heartbreak. Taking an 87-year-old woman out of her home after she had lived in the same house for 70 years, that’s killing someone. A year ago, she had such strength, such life, such enthusiasm. It was a joy to see her. And the moment she left that apartment, or, rather, the moment they took her out of that apartment, she had to be hospitalized. And today, she is gone.

So, breaking the news has been horrific, because most people here weren’t following the news. They were preparing food, helping people on the streets. It has been very hard. There have been many people crying, so many people trying to stay strong. But you can’t, not at a moment like this. …

Amid all this grief, I think it serves perfectly to show why we’re here, because we’re trying to fight so that no one has to feel that grief and that emptiness of feeling alone, and above all, so that people remember her, so that they remember that she died alone out of her home.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: Protesters also rallied in Barcelona on Wednesday to decry the death of Maricarmen.

PROTESTER: [translated] Maricarmen has died. But she didn’t just die. She was killed. The state killed her. The companies killed her. And she has been our inspiration. She’s pushed us even more to mobilize, to organize, to fight against those in power.

María, if you can talk about the significance of the death of MariCarmen, the response in the streets, and now what could lead to the fall of the Spanish government?

MARÍA CARRIÓN: Hi, Amy, Nermeen. Thank you so much for having me on.

Yes, Maricarmen has become a symbol, and it’s hard to believe that so much has happened in the last two weeks, since she was evicted on the 23rd of September after living in her home for over 70 years, and after activists had blocked the entrance to her building and her apartment with their own bodies, and resulting in massive police brutality, and then the images that have gone around the world of Maricarmen being taken out on a stretcher and into an ambulance and going into a hospital, where she’s been able to survive only for two weeks.

And this shows that what happens to vulnerable people and young people and people of every walk of life here in Spain when the interest of speculators is more important to those who govern than the well-being of ordinary citizens like Maricarmen. She literally put her body on the line for seven years, which is how long she fought this eviction for. And we’ve seen how she’s deteriorated over time, especially the last couple of weeks, but, really, since she began fighting for her home.

And so, she’s become a symbol, through her own loss of life, of the most extreme example of what happens to families and to individuals here whose homes are bought maybe by, you know, vulture funds or investment funds, and, like what happened to her, rent gets hiked by as much as five times what you can pay. This actual investment fund bought the apartment for very low cost because Maricarmen was living in it. It was a rent-controlled home, and they knew it very well, and that’s why the price was fixed so low. And then they proceeded to look for the way that they could legally expel her from her home.

And this is happening all over Spain. The same day that Maricarmen was evicted from her apartment, a family with two little kids was also evicted in Madrid. It’s a daily occurrence. And the encampments that have been born out of this outcry for what happened to Maricarmen, the people who are living on the streets now in small tents and putting their own bodies on the line, under, you know, rain and inclement weather, are saying this is enough.

And this is what has led to the protests. This is what led, finally, the Spanish government, which is considered quite progressive, to approve these housing decrees that got voted down in parliament. This is what resulted in last weekend’s massive protests all over Spain, which led Pedro Sánchez, the prime minister, on Monday to dissolve parliament and call for snap elections, and then proceed to approve these two decrees by a different system that happens once we don’t have a working parliament. And who knows what will happen from here to the 29th of November?

NERMEEN SHAIKH: So, María, before we conclude, if you could tell us who in Spain, what — is it a regional government, the state government — that is, the national government — or a municipal government that’s responsible for housing legislation and implementation?

MARÍA CARRIÓN: All of the above. So, we have national housing laws, which have to be approved by parliament. And in this case, these emergency decrees were not. But also, regional governments have to implement what the national governmental laws are. And in the case of conservative regional governments, including Madrid’s, which is extremely right-wing, they have refused to implement a lot of these housing laws.

But anyone, as the activists say, could have stepped in to prevent Maricarmen and so many other people from being evicted. So it’s a collective responsibility, which is why the street has said, “Enough. Everyone needs to be held responsible.” And all of these housing decrees are not even enough, because none of them basically are structural and go to the heart of the matter, which is that rents have gone up 80% in the last 10 years, while salaries have not kept up. Young people cannot leave their homes. They cannot become independent or start families. And this is what people are trying to change from the street.

AMY GOODMAN: I want to end with Maricarmen in her own words, speaking in May.

MARÍA DEL CARMEN ABASCAL MARTÍN: [translated] I’m 87 years old. I live on my own. I don’t have a family. And I have been living for 70 years in that house. A vulture fund bought it at the same price I would have been able to buy it. And in 2021, they took me to court because I have an old, lifelong rental contract. They tried to evict me in October 2025, and they stopped it. Now they will try to evict me on June 3rd. …

This government must understand people have the right to have a home, and they cannot evict people so vulture funds become rich without working.

AMY GOODMAN: That was Maricarmen speaking in May. She died on Wednesday. We thank María Carrión, independent journalist, joining us from Spain. And we will continue to cover this issue tomorrow on Democracy Now! Today, later tonight, there is a major march planned from the main plaza, where the encampments have been set up, to the apartment building where Maricarmen lived for over 70 years and was taken out by stretcher in her eviction, dying in the hospital on Wednesday.

A small New Jersey town once in the throes of the opioid crisis blew through more than $170,000 in settlement funds intended to fight drug addiction — to reportedly purchase pricey police SUVs and surveillance cameras.

Washington Township claimed it shelled out $170,446 on substance abuse initiatives in 2024 and 2025, but instead spent the money on 15 Flock cameras and two 2024 Chevrolet Tahoe SUVs, according to NJ.com.

“That’s absolutely egregious,” Sandy Gibson, an addiction specialist at The College of New Jersey, told the outlet.

“But I would hold the state accountable. We’re not auditing?”

Local officials also failed to use any of the money on drug abuse prevention in schools, which the well-documented settlement was intended for, records show.

The spending spree is part of a troubling pattern across the Garden State, where dozens of communities burned through at least $2.3 million in opioid settlement money on lavish purchases — like concerts, branded clothing and even a muscle car, according to an NJ.com probe.

Beginning in 2022, settlement funds from Big Pharma payouts — agreements totaling over $50 billion to resolve thousands of lawsuits against major companies tied to the pharmaceutical suppply chain — flowed into municipal coffers to offset the devastating toll the opioid epidemic inflicted on local communities.

The money was supposed to be used for education, prevention and treatment — but several New Jersey towns instead chose to upgraded streets, lighting and even purchased sleek new municipal gear.

Matthew Thomas Rooney, Washington Township solicitor, blamed the prior administration for any questionable purchases.

“The current administration is committed to transparency, and it will continue to review all budgeting priorities, including the best ways to help combat the opioid crisis … and will continue to work with the state on the best path forward,” Rooney told the publication in a statement.

“Nothing is more important to the current administration than keeping the people of Washington Township safe.”

Washington Township ranked among the worst 30% of New Jersey municipalities for addiction per capita during the height of the opioid crisis. In 2019, it recorded 5.78 cases per 1,000 people and 5.36 in 2021.

Gibson was appalled at the township’s inaction.

“I can’t see how there’s been no response or action taken to address that,” Gibson told NJ.com.

“Inaction at the level of the state is permission.”

The township claimed it spent $134,321 on a middle school “narcotics and education” program in 2024, followed by another $36,125 in 2025 earmarked for “early prevention.”

“These folks … they’re responsible for our tax dollars,” said resident Joe Junfola.

“To the extent that they get grants, such as the opioid funds, they’re tasked with using that money responsibly.”

Former Mayor Laurie Burns, a Democrat, slammed the town’s current Republican leadership for playing politics — and trying to “wash their hands” of the controversy.

“It’s a joke that the Washington Township’s Republican Mayor and Council would now try to wash their hands of decisions they made and point the finger elsewhere,” she wrote in an email.

“They did it, and they have a responsibility to answer for it now.”
