A small number of ABC devices were exposed to the malicious online ads. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

The ABC is wiping a small number of staff devices as a precaution but says it has found "no signs of compromise" from ads linked to a spyware campaign from an Israeli company.

Researchers uncovered an operation using online ads to infect devices, targeting Australian high-profile and sensitive organisations.

More than two dozen other Australian organisations are part of a "significant cluster" of targets, but they have not yet been identified.

The ABC has wiped staff devices that were exposed to a new, sophisticated cyber attack carried out as part of a broader campaign to track and even hack into networks of some of Australia's most high-profile and sensitive organisations.

It can be revealed the ABC is among more than two dozen Australian government, critical infrastructure, universities and media organisations that researchers claim were targeted by an Israel-based company abusing the online advertising system.

The public broadcaster confirmed a "small number" of devices had been exposed but said so far it had not identified any impact from the attack discovered by researchers at The Citizen Lab.

"The ABC is aware of the Citizen Lab report that describes exposure to advertising that may contain spyware. There is no evidence of a resulting compromise," a spokesperson said.

Know more about this story?

Email Cam Wilson on wilson.cameron@abc.net.au or his secure email cmwlsn@protonmail.com

The ABC attack was part of a bigger campaign, dubbed "Adfection", revealed by Citizen researchers last week.

The Canadian-based group found evidence that company Discover-Tech exploited digital advertising technology from major platforms like those run by Google to deliver spyware that could infect devices merely by viewing an online advertisement and without clicking.

Australia's nuclear science agency and other highly sensitive government organisations have been targeted by a sophisticated, foreign bad actor that secretly weaponised online ads to install spyware.

Researchers were able to confirm Discover-Tech's technique was used to infect devices at international news network Al Jazeera with spyware from another Israeli company, Candiru.

A spokesperson for the ABC confirmed that this had included the public broadcaster but had found no evidence so far of any adverse impact.

"Our review found that ads from this network were shown on a small number of ABC devices. We have found no evidence that any staff member has been identified or tracked," they said.

"For the small number of ABC devices identified, we have found no signs of compromise, and are wiping any still in service as a precaution. We take the privacy of staff and the protection of journalists' sources seriously."

Even if this infection is unsuccessful, researchers said, the same method also allowed the attackers to profile tens of millions of devices that were shown these malicious advertisements — measured by "impressions" — potentially giving information about their identities and online habits.

University of Queensland Professor Nicholas Carah, whose research focuses on digital advertising, said the attack was proof of the well-known risks about online advertising technology.

"On one level, it's horrifically surprisingly, but on another level it's like, well, yeah of course, online advertising is really useful infrastructure for doing something like this," he said.

Professor Nicholas Carah says the attack is proof of the risks about online advertising technology. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Professor Carah said the report showed how bad actors could exploit existing characteristics of online advertising technology to thwart protections that were supposed to stop tracking for nefarious purposes.

"You can get an [internet protocol] address, or a mobile, then, hey, presto, you're able to identify those individuals," he said.

Greens leader and digital rights spokesperson David Shoebridge said the report's contents were alarming.

"When foreign zero-click adtech is aimed at our public broadcaster, and other sensitive government agencies, that of course raises serious questions about foreign interference," he said, adding that this shows the need for privacy reform and to include advertising in the government's proposed digital duty of care.

While there were devices targeted across the world using Discover-Tech's techniques, Citizen Lab researchers noted a "substantial cluster of impressions in Australia, including on government and private-sector networks associated with critical infrastructure".

The researchers did not know who Discover-Lab or Candiru were carrying out the attacks on behalf of, if anyone.

Digicel Pacific's network resources are likely being used by private spy firms to track unsuspecting people on the other side of the world and steal their call, message and location data, according to an expert cybersecurity analysis.

The report singled out Australia's nuclear science agency, ANSTO, as being a hot spot in their data for the number of malicious ads shown. It did not specify the other organisations.

An ANSTO spokesperson told the ABC earlier this week it had not identified any impacts.

Australia's cybersecurity agency, the Australian Signals Directorate, declined to comment.

Researchers also claimed three Australian media organisations had seemingly been targets.

Media organisations and journalists are common targets for commercial spyware operations, alongside politicians, dissidents and human rights groups.

"The use of spyware against journalists is on the rise," international group Reporters Without Borders wrote late last year.

"Digital attacks often go unnoticed, so it is vital that journalists regularly check if their devices are compromised."

"For the small number of ABC devices identified, we have found no signs of compromise, and are wiping any still in service as a precaution. We take the privacy of staff and the protection of journalists' sources seriously."

Even if this infection is unsuccessful, researchers said, the same method also allowed the attackers to profile tens of millions of devices that were shown these malicious advertisements — measured by "impressions" — potentially giving information about their identities and online habits.

University of Queensland Professor Nicholas Carah, whose research focuses on digital advertising, said the attack was proof of the well-known risks about online advertising technology.

"On one level, it's horrifically surprisingly, but on another level it's like, well, yeah of course, online advertising is really useful infrastructure for doing something like this," he said.

Professor Nicholas Carah says the attack is proof of the risks about online advertising technology. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Professor Carah said the report showed how bad actors could exploit existing characteristics of online advertising technology to thwart protections that were supposed to stop tracking for nefarious purposes.

"You can get an [internet protocol] address, or a mobile, then, hey, presto, you're able to identify those individuals," he said.

Greens leader and digital rights spokesperson David Shoebridge said the report's contents were alarming.

"When foreign zero-click adtech is aimed at our public broadcaster, and other sensitive government agencies, that of course raises serious questions about foreign interference," he said, adding that this shows the need for privacy reform and to include advertising in the government's proposed digital duty of care.

While there were devices targeted across the world using Discover-Tech's techniques, Citizen Lab researchers noted a "substantial cluster of impressions in Australia, including on government and private-sector networks associated with critical infrastructure".

The researchers did not know who Discover-Lab or Candiru were carrying out the attacks on behalf of, if anyone.

Digicel Pacific's network resources are likely being used by private spy firms to track unsuspecting people on the other side of the world and steal their call, message and location data, according to an expert cybersecurity analysis.

The report singled out Australia's nuclear science agency, ANSTO, as being a hot spot in their data for the number of malicious ads shown. It did not specify the other organisations.

An ANSTO spokesperson told the ABC earlier this week it had not identified any impacts.

Australia's cybersecurity agency, the Australian Signals Directorate, declined to comment.

Researchers also claimed three Australian media organisations had seemingly been targets.

Media organisations and journalists are common targets for commercial spyware operations, alongside politicians, dissidents and human rights groups.

"The use of spyware against journalists is on the rise," international group Reporters Without Borders wrote late last year.

"Digital attacks often go unnoticed, so it is vital that journalists regularly check if their devices are compromised."

CEO of Argil AI Brivael Le Pogam discusses the widespread unrest, business damages and arrests ahead of upcoming demonstrations in Paris.

A suspected terrorist attack near Paris Friday added to tensions across France as the nation prepares for more potential violence Saturday.

Seventy thousand law enforcement officers, along with helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons, will be deployed across France as President Emmanuel Macron’s government tries to ward off another weekend of violent protests.

"The strategy adopted for the coming days is to ban protests requested by individuals or groups with no legitimate authority," Macron said ahead of the weekend after canceling his planned trip to Nigeria and Senegal originally scheduled for next week.

"The rules are simple, and I think they're just common sense," Macron added. "The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days."

FRANCE'S MACRON BLAMES PROTESTS ON 'ULTRA-LEFT GROUPS WHOSE AIM IS TO BRING DOWN THE REPUBLIC'

Protesters marched through central Paris amid clashes, fires and heavy police deployment during nationwide demonstrations against rising living costs in Paris, France, Oct. 17, 2026 (Firas Abdullah/Anadolu via Getty Images)

"Where trade unions submit requests to hold demonstrations, prefects will examine them in accordance with the law," he added, "but alternative routes will be proposed" to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings.

Adding to security concerns, a suspected terrorist attack occurred in the city of Trappes, west of Paris. A 39-year-old man was arrested by police after one person was killed and four others, including a 12-year-old girl, were wounded in what was originally said to be a "relatively random" shooting.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has since told local media, "The motive may be racist. The investigation is ongoing, but this is clearly a terrorist crime."

The AFP reported the suspect appeared to fire randomly from a vehicle, and the mayor told reporters the dead victim and at least one of the wounded were "of African origin."

Macron said "the nation is standing with" the victims of this "terrible ordeal."

FRANCE COULD FACE EVEN WORSE DESTRUCTION WITH SECOND WEEKEND OF PLANNED RIOTS, STATE DEPT WARNS

Riot police officers run across a street during protests in Paris, France, Oct. 17, 2026. (Bruno Camillo/Reuters)

Ahead of Saturday's protests and after acknowledging that police had "lost control" during last weekend's unrest, Nuñez, the interior minister, said his ministry is "ready for tomorrow. We will be extremely vigilant, extremely firm, and we will let absolutely nothing pass."

Reuters reports that the Union Nationale des Étudiants de France, or UNEF, one of the nation’s oldest student unions, has said its planned rallies will go on as scheduled despite police rejecting their permit requests. Police have so far only approved a union demonstration in Paris, Reuters reported, while denying requests from UNEF and the "Yellow Vest" movement, an anti-establishment force that first emerged in 2018.

Macron also took aim at those he says are behind the violence, saying, "Last Saturday, we had political and seditious acts by ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic."

Riot police stand together outside the Pitié-Salpêtrière hospital (13th arrondissement) in Paris on Thursday, Oct.22, 2026,  (Jan Schmidt-Whitley/Le Pictorium via Reuters)

Earlier this week, Fabian Vanhemelryck, secretary general of the Alliance Police Nationale union, said political figures deserved blame because of "those who excuse the inexcusable, justify violence and prefer to overwrite police officers rather than condemn those who attack them."

He also said the "state that abandons its police officers in the face of increasingly uninhibited violence, while demanding that they accept, remain(s) silent and continue(s) to hold the line."

Major French institutions, like the Louvre and the Musée d'Orsay, will be closed in anticipation of Saturday’s planned protests, and 24 Metro stations across Paris will be closed. A Ligue 1 soccer match between Paris Saint-Germain and Olympique Lyonnais, scheduled for Sunday night at Parc des Princes in the capital, has also been postponed to Monday evening.

French President Emmanuel Macron, center, hosts an Interministerial Crisis Meeting at the Elysee Presidential Palace in Paris Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026, the day after nationwide riots. (Ludovic Marin/Pool Photo via AP)

The NFL game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the New Orleans Saints, scheduled for Sunday afternoon at Stade de France just north of central Paris, is still set to be played as scheduled, yet some weekend events around the game have been canceled.

The Stade de France is the same stadium that hosted an international soccer match between France and neighboring Germany during the Nov. 13, 2015 terror attacks.

Explosions were heard outside the stadium during the game that night, with then-French President François Hollande in attendance. Fans were held inside the stadium for hours while authorities dealt with the attacks unfolding around Paris that night.

The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

Brooklyn community groups are urging voters to reject Proposal 3, a Mayor Zohran Mamdani-backed charter change on the Nov. 3 ballot that would make it harder to stop street redesigns.

The coalition of 11 groups, led by Brooklyn for All of Us and Our Communities Count, will rally Saturday at 10 a.m. outside Barclays Center.

“We are not against safer streets. We are against decisions being made about our communities without meaningful participation from the people who live and work here,” organizers said in a press release.

The DOT is backing the new ballot proposal because it will give them more leeway to push ahead with street projects.

Proposal 3 would prevent technical errors from being grounds to stop construction and allow DOT to begin certain projects before presenting them to local officials and community boards.

But organizers argue the agency’s plans ignore the needs of families, small businesses, seniors and people with disabilities.

The groups want the DOT to reverse previous decisions which they say have been made without meaningful community input.   They are also calling for a halt to proposed bike boulevards on Bergen and Dean streets and Lafayette and DeKalb avenues — plus a stop to Mamdani’s new “Fast Bus Lanes” across Brooklyn, a joint DOT-MTA plan that in part eliminates bus stops.

The administration has claimed the charter changes will help with street safety.

A spokesperson for DOT said the agency is trying to deliver “high-quality, affordable transportation.”

“We look forward to listening to and working with the community to ensure these investments reflect the needs of the people who call these neighborhoods home,” a spokesperson for DOT said.

The coalition’s main message was that they want to be heard.

“Our streets belong to everyone—pedestrians, cyclists, bus riders, motorists, seniors, families, and local merchants. Every voice deserves to be heard before permanent changes are made,” organizers said.

perspective-midterm-money-madness:
Scott Simon

Troy Jackson (D) directs a question to Sen. Susan Collins (R) during the final Maine U.S. Senate debate in Bangor, Maine, Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026.
                
                    
                    Gregory A. Rec/Pool Portland Press Herald/AP
                    
                
                hide caption

Campaign spending for these midterm elections passed 10 billion dollars this week, according to the tracking group AdImpact.

Maybe we should repeat that number: $10 billion dollars.

The senate race in Ohio, for example, has already cost more than $460 million in combined ad spending. The Texas Senate race has surpassed half a billion. Then there's $260 million more in the Maine Senate race.

The most expensive House race in the country isn't in California or New York, but Michigan's 7th congressional district with nearly $60 million in ads. Contests in Iowa and Florida are just under $50 million apiece.

There are limits on personal campaign contributions in the United States--but, since the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision in 2010, no limits on donations to "super PACs," which can publicly support or oppose candidates but can't directly coordinate with campaigns. Rich donors have used that ruling to steer hundreds of millions of dollars to support both parties, up and down the ballot. Elon Musk alone has given $276 million to Republican groups, just since July. George Soros has given more than $100 million dollars to Democrats this election cycle.

Meanwhile, voters, whom politicians are trying to win over with all these ads, tell pollsters and reporters that their top issues this fall are the economy and the cost of living. Inflation is up; gas prices have spiked since the start of the Iran war; groceries cost a third more than they did in 2019.

It is hard not to wonder: what could those hundreds of millions of ad dollars accomplish if they went toward food, gas, or shelter for those in need, or to help people with health care costs? Could some of it pay for school nurses, music teachers, and librarians? Subsidize addiction care? Clean up public parks?

Maybe a candidate could win support these days by declaring, "And I vow to spend less money on my campaign than my opponent!" After all, as the Los Angeles Dodgers might remind us this week, spending the most money doesn't always deliver victory.
